title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what the evidence proves, where the future comes from, and why a story holds

questions.prompt: Your module sorts the threats to the environment into two columns. Three of these six belong in the column of natural disasters and three are put down to human activity. Which three are the natural ones?

options.text: acid rain
a drought
deforestation
an earthquake
a garbage dump
a volcanic eruption

questions.explanation: Put the same question to each of the six: would this still happen if nobody lived here? A drought would — the sky simply withholds its rain for a long enough period to damage the crops. An earthquake would — strained rocks in the crust break and rebound whether or not anybody is standing on them. A volcanic eruption would — a vent opens and expels lava, steam and ash. The other three exist only because of what people do. Deforestation is the cutting down of a forest, and somebody does the cutting. A garbage dump is where a town leaves what it throws away. And acid rain is the hardest of the six, which is why it is here: the rain itself is perfectly natural, but the acid in it comes from the sulphur and nitrogen that factories and vehicles put into the air, so your module files it on the man-made side. Notice that all six are threats to the environment: the word covers both columns, and telling one column from the other is what the sorting is for.

questions.prompt: The study-based text of your module reports clear evidence that global warming is caused by human activity, and then says that many world leaders have closed their ears to that finding. It gives their reason in so many words. What is it?

options.text: They do not trust the instruments the researchers used.
They have not yet been shown the findings of the new study.
They think the study needs to be repeated elsewhere.
They would have to spend money or slow their economies.

questions.explanation: The text puts the reason immediately after the fact and ties the two together with so: the leaders have closed their ears to it so that they do not have to limit their economic activity or introduce expensive pollution controls. Money and growth, in other words — and the text adds that this is one of the reasons America has not signed the Kyoto Treaty on climate change. The three others are objections a scientist might raise about the study itself, and the text raises none of them: it calls the evidence clear, says the findings remove much of the uncertainty that surrounded the debate, and reports that the researchers can already simulate both the past and the likely future evolution of the warming. Read the sentence for what the writer accuses the leaders of, not for what a careful reader might object.

questions.prompt: Two lines from a council report on the same reservoir. (1) "If the drought holds until August, the town will be short of water." (2) "The level has dropped nine metres since March; the reservoir is going to run dry." What does the change from will to be going to tell the reader?

options.text: That the second is a plan the council has made.
That the second is further away in time.
That the second is less certain than the first.
That the second rests on measured figures.

questions.explanation: Your book separates the two forms by where the future comes from. will carries something the writer expects — here a consequence he works out from a condition that has not even been met yet, if the drought holds. be going to carries a prediction read off evidence that is already there for anybody to point at, and the report supplies it in the same breath: nine metres, measured since March. Nothing makes the second sentence further away in time; if anything the figures bring it nearer. Nothing makes it less certain either — the evidence is exactly what makes it more so. And a plan is something somebody intends to bring about, which no council intends of a reservoir running dry.

questions.prompt: A survey team reaches a valley the morning after a night of rain and writes four sentences in its notebook. Only one of them is a deduction about the past of the kind your module teaches. Which one?

options.text: The bridge is under a metre of water.
The river must be flowing at four metres a second.
The river must have burst its bank before midnight.
We must have the road cleared before the lorries come.

questions.explanation: Only one sentence concludes something about a moment already over, and it does it with the module's own structure, must plus have plus a past participle: nobody watched the bank give way, and the conclusion is drawn from what the valley looks like this morning. The line about the bridge is not a conclusion at all — it states what the team can see, and it is the very evidence a conclusion would rest on. The line about four metres a second does contain must and is a deduction, but must be points at what is happening now, not at what happened earlier. And the line about the road is the trap: the words must have are there, yet have is the ordinary verb, and what follows the noun is a past participle — cleared — so the sentence lays an obligation on the team: we must get the road cleared. A past participle alone after must have gives you a deduction; a noun followed by a past participle gives you something quite different.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes: "When Karim reached the crossroads, the road ___ hours before, and he had to turn back." The road is the thing the action was done to, and that action was over before he arrived. Which form fills the gap?

options.text: had been closed
had closed
has been closed
was closed

questions.explanation: Two demands are made of one form. The road did not close anything; it is what somebody closed, so the verb has to be passive, be plus a past participle. And the closing was finished before Karim arrived, which is itself in the past, so the earlier of the two past moments takes the past perfect. Stack the two and be goes into the past perfect: had been closed — the same shape as the sentence in your book's own text, where a school had already been engulfed. had closed is a past perfect but active, and it makes the road the thing that did the closing. was closed is passive and correctly in the past, but it puts the two moments on the same level, so nothing says the road was already shut when he got there. And has been closed ties the closing to the present moment, which cannot stand in a story told in the past.

questions.prompt: A pupil hands in her story of the flood. It runs: the water came in at four in the morning; the family climbed to the roof; a neighbour's boat took them off at seven; they slept in the school hall. Her teacher writes underneath: "Everything happens, but nothing is explained." Which sentence, added to the story, answers that comment?

options.text: At seven in the morning the boat came round the corner.
The drain under the road had been blocked all spring.
The family had never spent a night away from the house.
The water was cold and black, and it smelt of the river.

questions.explanation: The teacher's comment is about cause. The story lists what happened, in the right order and in the right tenses, and never once says why any of it happened. The blocked drain supplies the missing link — the water had nowhere to go, so it came into the house — and that is precisely the link your module asks you to build into a narrative, the one between a cause and an effect. The sentence about the boat adds a fifth event to a story that already has four, and it repeats a time the story has given you. The sentence about the night away and the sentence about the cold black water are both good writing, but they are description: they make the reader see and feel, which is the other thing the section asks for, and neither of them explains anything. A story needs both jobs done — description so that the reader can picture it, causation so that the reader can follow it.
